intro: Norwich is the county city of Norfolk, and its Norman cathedral, begun in 1096, stands in a walled close that once covered a tenth of the medieval city. In the grass of the close, by the cathedral's east end, a broad cedar of Lebanon spreads its tiers under the spire. A reader sent it to us with their own photograph.
meta_description: A cedar of Lebanon in the close of Norwich Cathedral, under the second tallest spire in England, free to walk past.

trees.name: The Norwich Cathedral Cedar

location.address: The Close, Norwich Cathedral, Norwich NR1 4DD, by the east end of the cathedral

trees.story:
A reader sent us this cedar of Lebanon with one line, "In the grounds of Norwich Cathedral", and a photograph that explains why it stopped them. The tree stands beside a gravel path in the cathedral close, its dark, layered branches sweeping out low over the grass, and behind it rise the rounded Norman east end of the cathedral and its stone spire, half lost in mist.

The cathedral was begun in 1096. Its spire, built in 1480, is the second tallest in England at 96 metres. The cedar is far younger than either, but we have found no record of when it was planted or how big its trunk is, so this page gives it no age rather than guess one.

What the photograph does show is a broad, heavy tree with a straight dark trunk and great flat tiers of needles, standing on its own in the grass of the close, with a pale stone sculpture of a mother and child a few steps away. The close is open to walk through, and the tree is seen from the path. If you know when it was planted, or have put a tape round its trunk, tell us on this page.

question_meta: The cedar in Norwich Cathedral's close: where it stands and what is known about it.
question_answer: A cedar of Lebanon stands in the close of Norwich Cathedral, by the cathedral's east end under the spire. Its planting date and size are not recorded in any source we found.
question_context: A cedar of Lebanon grows in the close of Norwich Cathedral, in the grass beside a gravel path near the cathedral's rounded east end, with a pale stone sculpture of a mother and child a few steps away. A reader sent it to us with a photograph of the tree under the spire, and we have found no record of when it was planted or how big its trunk is, so the page gives it no age. Norwich Cathedral is the Church of England cathedral of Norwich in Norfolk. Building began in 1096 under Herbert de Losinga, the first bishop, and the structure is mostly Norman, of flint and mortar faced with cream Caen limestone. When the Norman church was finished it was the largest building in East Anglia. The stone spire, built in 1480 to replace a wooden one, is the second tallest in England at 96 metres, and the cloisters, begun in 1297, are the fourth largest in England. The close around the cathedral once covered a tenth of the medieval city. It is open to walk through, and the cedar is seen from the path.
